intro:
On Las Olas Boulevard and along the water, dozens of restaurants sit within a few blocks of each other, and many of the people walking past your door have never heard of you. They decide where to eat on their phones, by searching and reading reviews. And if your restaurant has slower months, those same tables can sit half empty on a Tuesday.

That is the challenge of running a restaurant in Fort Lauderdale. You are competing with the spot next door, trying to get found by visitors who do not know the city, winning them over in the few seconds they spend on their phone, and keeping your dining room full in the slower weeks. It is a different job than marketing a neighborhood spot that lives on regulars.

This guide is for owners who are tired of guessing. We will cover what actually makes marketing a restaurant in Fort Lauderdale different, what your restaurant really needs from marketing here, what to look for in a restaurant marketing agency in Fort Lauderdale, and how our team at Button Up Media helps local restaurants turn searches and scrolls into booked tables.

sections.h2: What makes marketing a Fort Lauderdale restaurant different?
sections.html:
Marketing a restaurant in Fort Lauderdale has its own challenges, and they come down to a few things.

The water matters. Fort Lauderdale calls itself the Yachting Capital of the World, and with the Intracoastal, the New River, and the canals, some guests at a waterfront restaurant arrive by boat. Waterfront rooms from Las Olas to the beach compete on views as much as food, so your photos and your online presence have to sell the view as well as the plate.

The competition sits shoulder to shoulder. Las Olas Boulevard has a lot of restaurants in a short, walkable strip, and Himmarshee and the downtown Riverwalk add more. Being the best food on the block does not help if the person scrolling their phone never lands on your name.

Your crowd may change with the calendar. If you get more visitors in the winter months and fewer the rest of the year, a restaurant that only markets when it is already busy leaves money on the table in the busy months and struggles to fill seats in the slow ones.

Your guests may be a real mix. On one night you might serve visitors from out of state, a table of boaters, and locals, some of whom prefer Spanish. That mix is why a one-language, one-note approach falls flat.

The neighborhoods are not interchangeable. An upscale room on Las Olas, a lively spot in the historic Himmarshee nightlife district, a trendy cafe in Flagler Village and the FAT Village arts area, and a beachfront place off A1A are all marketing to different people in different moods. The message that works for one misses the others.

sections.h2: What does a Fort Lauderdale restaurant actually need from marketing?
sections.html:
Forget the buzzwords for a minute. In this city, a handful of things do almost all the heavy lifting. Here is what matters, in plain terms.

  • A Google Business Profile that wins 'near me.' When a tourist on the beach or a boater at the dock types 'waterfront restaurant near me' or 'best dinner Fort Lauderdale,' Google decides who shows up on the map. Your profile, your categories, your photos, and your reviews decide whether that is you or the place down the street. For a restaurant that lives on visitors, this is the single most valuable thing to get right.
  • Reviews, and replies to them. Visitors who do not know the city lean hard on reviews. A steady flow of fresh, strong reviews, with real replies (in English and Spanish), is often the deciding factor between two patios on the same block.
  • Social content that sells the experience. Food, yes, but also the water, the patio, the golden hour, the vibe. Short video does the heavy lifting now. Good content gives a visitor a reason to choose you and gives a local a reason to come back.
  • A website that works on a phone. Nearly every visitor checks you on their phone first. They want the menu, hours, a photo, a map, and a way to book or find parking (or dockage) in a few taps. A slow or clunky site quietly sends people elsewhere.
  • Ads you can turn up and down. Google and Meta ads let you push harder in your busy months and lean on locals to fill the slower ones. Done right, ads help you make the most of busy weeks and get through the quiet ones.

You do not need all of this perfect on day one. You need a partner who knows which lever to pull first for your room, your neighborhood, and the time of year.

sections.h2: How should a Fort Lauderdale restaurant market around the season and the big events?
sections.html:
If your restaurant has busy and slow months, plan your marketing around them instead of reacting a week too late.

Build the foundation before your busy months. The weeks before your busy stretch are when you want your Google profile polished, your reviews flowing, your photos fresh, and your ads tested. When the visitors arrive, everything is already running and you can focus on serving them.

Treat the big moments as real opportunities. The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show in the fall is billed as the largest in-water boat show in the world. The Winterfest Boat Parade runs along the water in December, and Tortuga Music Festival takes place on the beach in the spring. Each one is a chance to run a themed promotion, a timed ad push, and content aimed at people who are in town and looking for somewhere to eat tonight.

Do not go dark in your slow months. When visitor traffic drops, leaning on locals pays off. Loyalty offers, slow-night promotions, and content aimed at Broward residents (in both languages) keep your dining room from feeling the drop as hard. The goal is a steadier year.

This kind of planning is hard to do off the side of your desk during service. It is a big part of what a local agency actually earns its fee doing.

sections.h2: Do you really need a local agency, or will any agency do?
sections.html:
Plenty of agencies can work with a Fort Lauderdale restaurant from far away, and a lot of marketing work, like ads, websites, and SEO, does not depend on where the agency sits. Some parts still go better with local knowledge and people on the ground.

A team that knows the area knows that a Las Olas room and a Flagler Village cafe are marketing to different people, and it will plan your year around the Boat Show, Winterfest, and your own busy and slow months. A crew that can film in person also makes it easier to keep fresh photos and video coming.

You do not need a local agency for everything. For content shot in person, bilingual content, and planning around local events, it helps to work with people who know Fort Lauderdale. We are headquartered in Miami, and we film in person in Fort Lauderdale.

faqs.a: Keep marketing when visitor traffic drops, and lean on locals. That means loyalty offers, slow-night and happy-hour promotions, content aimed at Broward residents in both languages, and ads targeted at people who live here year-round. Planning for the quiet months ahead of time gives you a steadier year than only marketing when you are already full.

faqs.q: How should a waterfront restaurant market to boaters and tourists?
faqs.a: Visitors and boaters usually decide on their phones, so your online presence has to do the selling. That means a Google profile and website that clearly show your location, dockage or parking, hours, and menu, plus photos and short video that capture the water, the patio, and the view as well as the food. Strong, recent reviews matter even more with people who do not know the city. Tying promotions to big waterfront moments like the Boat Show and Winterfest helps you catch visitors when they are actively looking for somewhere to eat.

faqs.q: How long does restaurant marketing take to work in Fort Lauderdale?
faqs.a: Some things move fast and some take time. A cleaned-up Google Business Profile and a focused ad campaign can lift calls and visits within weeks, especially heading into your busy months. Local SEO, review growth, and social momentum build over a few months. Any agency promising to double your sales overnight is guessing. A good partner sets honest expectations, fixes the foundations first, and then builds momentum, with results compounding over the following months.
